query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A moderate warm-forging step at approximately 800–900 °C followed by a short sub-critical anneal will partially spheroidize and refine the lamellar colony interfaces in the eutectic HEA, thereby reducing interfacial stress concentrations that trigger premature microcracking. This processing modification will improve both the ultimate tensile strength and room-temperature ductility compared to the unmodified as-cast lamellar-colony baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure possessing numerous internal boundaries that serve as sites for microcrack nucleation under room-temperature tensile loads.
generation.intervention: A controlled thermal/thermomechanical treatment comprising a moderate warm-forging pass at ~800–900 °C followed by a short sub-critical annealing (or aging) step.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile deformation (standard tensile test conditions) with processing maintained below the full recrystallization temperature to preserve the refined lamellar framework.
generation.structural_mediator: Partial spheroidization and refinement of the inter-lamellar boundaries that reduces stress concentration sites within the dual-phase lamellar colonies.
generation.mechanism: The warm forging at elevated temperature promotes plastic flow that slightly reduces the inter-lamellar spacing and changes the lamellar interface morphology; the subsequent sub-critical annealing stabilizes this refined structure. Together, these steps enable enhanced dislocation transmission and reduce stress concentrations that initiate microcracking, thereby simultaneously increasing tensile strength (through dislocation-based strengthening) and ductility (by mitigating premature interfacial failure).
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, the treated alloy is expected to exhibit an approximate ≥20% increase in ultimate tensile strength and a ≥10% improvement in elongation at fracture, due to decreased microcrack initiation and propagation.
generation.baseline: The as-cast eutectic HEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure that shows microcracking along internal colony boundaries leading to brittle failure and limited tensile ductility.
generation.boundary: The intervention is effective when the forging temperature remains in the ~800–900 °C range (high enough to aid plastic deformation but below the full recrystallization threshold) and the annealing time is controlled to avoid over-coarsening of the microstructure. Excessive temperature or time could negate the benefits by degrading the refined lamellar architecture.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the strength and ductility enhancements is subject to variation based on the precise thermal cycle parameters and initial microstructural characteristics. Additional microstructural characterization is required to optimize processing conditions and confirm the reduction in microcrack formation.

falsification_experiment.design: Process two sets of identical as-cast eutectic HEA specimens: one set receiving the proposed warm-forging (800–900 °C) plus short sub-critical anneal treatment, and a control set with no additional treatment. Perform room-temperature tensile tests on both sets. Perform microstructural analysis (e.g., SEM or TEM) to assess inter-lamellar spacing, spheroidization, and microcrack density.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the processed specimens do not exhibit at least a 20% increase in UTS and a 10% increase in ductility compared to the baseline, or if microstructural analysis shows no significant reduction in stress concentration sites (e.g., similar interfacial microcrack density and lamellar morphology) relative to the untreated specimens.

Figure 4a–c, e reveal that dislocations cut through the δ-lamellae, yet are pinned by the γ ″ particles. For the coherent δ-lamellae structure, as the tensile stress increases up to the yield stress, dislocation slip occurs in the fcc matrix and involves shearing across the δ-lamellae, which indicates an early stage of the planar dislocation slip across the coherent δ/γ boundaries (Fig. 4a ). With further increase in strain to 10%, slip bands can clearly be observed across the δ-lamellae (Fig. 4b ). At a strain of 14%, shearing of the δ-lamellae by the slip bands leads to a large local shear (~40%) (Fig. 4c ), rather than the creation of a crack, which alleviates the local stress concentration. A schematic diagram of the interaction of dislocations with δ-lamellae is shown in Fig. 4d .

decision.trend: In the only directly relevant study (PMC4145285), researchers investigated an as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA with a fine lamellar (fcc/B2) microstructure to improve both fracture strength and ductility. Although cold rolling bolstered the alloy’s strength, it sacrificed ductility. The as-cast lamellar architecture offered moderate tensile strength along with notable elongation at room temperature, but cracking at lamellar boundaries remained a problem for further improvement in ductility. While the study demonstrated that a refined inter-lamellar spacing could yield high strength and reasonable elongation, the brittleness from internal boundary cracking persisted and was not fully solved.
decision.unsolved: Despite controlling inter-lamellar spacing via casting and limited cold deformation, microcracks still form and propagate along lamellar boundaries. Retaining or increasing strength while significantly improving room-temperature ductility has not been conclusively achieved in such eutectic HEAs. A key challenge is to mitigate boundary-driven cracking without undermining the architectural advantages conferred by the lamellar structure.
decision.lever: Introduce a moderate warm-forging step at ~800–900 °C followed by a short sub-critical anneal or aging treatment to partially spheroidize and stabilize fine lamellae, thereby reducing boundary stress concentrations and enhancing toughening mechanisms.
decision.why: Testable hypothesis: A controlled warm-forging pass reduces inter-lamellar spacing and drives partial spheroidization of the B2/fcc interfaces, mitigating stress concentrations that trigger microcracks. The subsequent mild aging further refines and stabilizes the microstructure, enabling dislocation-based strengthening along with improved slip transfer. Relative to an unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, the outcome should be higher ultimate tensile strength (≥20% gain) coupled with improved ductility (≥10% elongation increase). Suitable boundary conditions include a forging temperature high enough to aid plastic flow but below full recrystallization onset to preserve a refined lamellar framework. Prior results (PMC4145285) show that refining lamellar features and controlling their morphology can improve strength and ductility, supporting this approach. A falsifying experiment would observe unchanged or worsened ductility (e.g., <25% elongation) if microcracks still initiate and quickly propagate despite warm forming and sub-critical annealing.
